summary.title: Big O
summary.one_liner: Big O notation describes how a function's running time grows with input size, illustrated with visual examples of constant, logarithmic, linear, and quadratic algorithms.
keywords: how do i analyze algorithm performance
why is my code slow with large inputs
takeaways: Big O describes how running time grows as input size grows, not the absolute time taken.
Common categories from fastest to slowest growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n^2).
Bubble sort is O(n^2) in the worst case; binary search is O(log n).
Calling indexOf inside a loop turns an O(n) loop into O(n^2); using indexes or a Set/Map can reduce cost.
Caching intermediate results with a Map can speed up average case without changing worst-case complexity.
summary.summary: The article introduces big O notation as a way to describe how wall-clock time grows with input size, rather than measuring time directly. It uses interactive JavaScript examples to show linear sum loops versus constant-time formula versions, then covers bubble sort (O(n^2)) and binary search (O(log n)). The final sections apply these ideas to practical fixes: choosing Set or Map for lookups, avoiding indexOf inside loops, and caching factorial results.
